text: Before naming a single AWS service, write down what Finance's request actually requires: the same logic running every time, a destination built for repeated joins, and loose typing fixed once, centrally, instead of redone differently by every consumer.

That points to one plan. The existing raw catalog table feeds a Glue ETL job called northfield-orders-etl, which cleans and types the data and writes it as Parquet into a curated S3 zone. From there, a COPY step loads it into the Redshift warehouse, northfield-analytics, landing in one fact table and three dimension tables.

Two choices are worth calling out. First, the ETL job writes to a curated S3 zone instead of straight into Redshift, because that output is reusable by Athena later and because re-running a load doesn't mean re-running the whole Spark job. Second, the warehouse is Redshift Serverless, because Northfield's queries spike around month-end and go quiet the rest of the time, and Serverless bills per RPU-second instead of charging for an always-on cluster.

The warehouse itself, previewed before Lesson 4 builds it in full, is a small, deliberate star schema: one fact table at the order-line grain, and three dimension tables carrying exactly the descriptive attributes Finance and Ops will actually filter and group by. Nothing more than their real reports require.
Next lesson: the real PySpark code behind northfield-orders-etl, line by line, so you can see exactly how the raw, untyped data gets cleaned on its way into the curated zone.
